<meta>continues from previous page: ...the time it spends in the fire requires careful attention, and the gradual succession of that increase, with caution, until its lime is fixed, lest it easily return into a body, so that a greater fire may be administered to it for the perfection of its lime. Similarly, let it not happen that one errs with <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss>, because of the difficulty of its reduction, so that if at any time one places its lime into reduction, it happens to him that it does not reduce, but rather he finds it in its former disposition or reduced to glass, and he judges its reduction impossible. For we say that if one does not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If, however, he applies a great one, it does not necessarily follow that it will reduce, but it is possible that he may reduce it into vitrification <note>glass-making process</note>. And that is because <term>Jupiter</term> has a fugitive substance of <term>argentum uiuum</term> <gloss>quicksilver/mercury</gloss> enclosed in the depth of its nature. If it drags out a long stay in the fire, it will flee, and it will leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found to be more fit for vitrification than for conversion into the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own humidity gives no fusion except a vitrifying one. And therefore it is necessarily left that, with a most rapid force of fire, one must hasten to reduce it quickly. Otherwise, it will not be reduced. Therefore, let him exercise himself in this, and he will know.

The <gloss>second</gloss> mode of calcination of these two bodies, <gloss>Saturn</gloss> <gloss>Lead</gloss> <gloss>and Jupiter</gloss>, which is perfected by the acuteness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown over their face, after a quantity very often in its fusion, and let it be mixed by much agitation with an iron rod, over the fire, until they are turned into ash by the mixture of salt. And afterwards, let their lime be perfected by the same mode of perfection, with its considerations. But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>plumbum</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> is converted into powder more easily from the first labors of calcination than <term>Jupiter</term>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>lead</gloss> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.</meta>

<summary>This passage describes the technical challenges in reducing the calcined metals of lead and tin, specifically emphasizing the risk of vitrification due to the loss of mercury, and details a method for calcination using salt.</summary>
<keywords>calcination, Jupiter, tin, Saturn, lead, vitrification, mercury, salt, reduction, metallurgy</keywords>
